P2: I bring up vaccination because it's one of the values that would decide whether I could raise children in a community at all. It's not like I'm trying to design a village for everybody, but a certain amount of agreement on children's health is necessary before parents can actually trust one another.
P3: The review from a now grown child matters more than founders usually want it to. Adults can go on forever about what they intended. The person who actually lived through the system may eventually tell a different story.
P5: A friend who reviewed this draft grew up in a Christian commune in Colorado where her father was a pastor. She calls her childhood "a treasure and a burden." A treasure because she belonged, and everybody cared for everybody. A burden because of the strict religious life she had no say in.
P6: What she said is more useful than another promo video showing kids smiling and carrying vegetables.
P7: My view is that moms should raise their own kids, inside a community where the care is really shared. The village can handle meals, supervision, teaching, protection, playing, and a lot of the fathering, but it should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.
P8: A big part of why I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's [*The Continuum Concept*](https://www.arvindguptatoys.com/arvindgupta/conconcept.pdf). Keep in mind that it's one outsider's interpretation of the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing what she saw. Still, it's a powerful picture. In her account, babies are carried along in ordinary adult life. Children are around people of several ages and learn by taking part, and a single exhausted parent isn't expected to be a child's whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.
P9: Experiments with kids sleeping and living apart from their parents need to be approached with special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that [communal sleeping for children eventually came to an end, due to a combination of developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12395568/). Kids can benefit from high-quality group care, and from having several loving adults around, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.
P10: Tamera's Children's Place deserves to be studied directly, not caricatured. Personally, I'm still biased toward systems that open up a kid's circle without making the bond between parent and child ideologically inconvenient.
P11: Kids also need their own territory, a space to create their own society in, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.
P12: I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it's still one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG's *Kinderhaus* works from a similar idea. The adults take care of safety on the outside, but the kids still get a world of their own.
P13: Because this can be badly misunderstood, the safeguards have to be spelled out. A children's territory can't become a place where adults stop paying attention. It can't be a place where older kids quietly dominate younger ones, or where secrecy gets treated as a sign of independence.
P14: I also don't buy the suburban paranoia that treats any warm relationship between a kid and a grownup who isn't related to them as suspect. It's good for a child to know and be known by lots of grownups who enjoy them, who would notice when something changes, and who would act when something's wrong. That kind of fear can destroy the gift without actually preventing abuse.
P16: Give children real agency. Their "no" matters. No grown-up has a right to a child's affection, physical contact, obedience beyond what legitimate safety requires, or private access to them.
P17: Have a no-secrets rule. No grown-up may ever ask a child to keep a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation, or a relationship secret from the child's mother or another trusted adult. A surprise needs an end date. Secrets meant to isolate the child aren't allowed.
P18: Teach kids to be truthful before there's a crisis. They should know that what they say is powerful, and that adults will listen seriously. That teaching must never turn into an interrogation, punishment for not being sure, or a reason to dismiss what a child reports. A scared or confused child may not tell the story perfectly, and still need protecting.
P19: Hear the child even when the person accused is someone people love. That's where communities fail, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or just everybody's friend. Decide on the process for responding ahead of time, before anyone's face is attached to it. First, make sure everyone is safe right away. Then see that a competent and fair investigation is done, and that nothing gets hushed up because of anybody's status.
P20: Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities [seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid](https://vtdigger.org/2024/06/21/40-years-later-island-pond-has-little-interest-in-revisiting-its-historic-raid/), and a court returned them after rejecting the state's blanket request. State intervention can fail spectacularly. A community that closes itself off completely can also fail. Children need more than one world.
P21: I also searched [the research corpus](https://innerself.185-233-106-15.sslip.io/blog/commune-article-research/) for a well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, where the record follows the whole sequence of events: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I didn't find one. That may be because records are private, or because cases were sent elsewhere, but it means I can't claim that communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
P22: Amish young people decide for themselves, as adults, whether or not to join the church, and [roughly 85 percent or more eventually do](https://groups.etown.edu/amishstudies/social-organization/population-growth/). Popular culture has blown *Rumspringa* out of proportion, as if every teenager went wild, but adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.
P23: If a community's children never leave, how can it know whether they'd freely come back? Let them study, travel, make friends, run into other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
P24: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary parents aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." They'll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
P25: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. Kids who grow up without using money especially need to know enough about how the money world works that they aren't helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help. They need skills and an education they can take with them, relationships outside the community, access to their records and documents, and at least one plausible next step, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community can help out with temporary housing, travel, tools, or a small reserve for the transition, great. But even if it can't, it can at least avoid punishing people for leaving, or withholding the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing gives perfect freedom. The point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
P26: Some may leave for good, and others may start their own communities with different values instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.
P27: Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, [schooling](https://www.instagram.com/p/DcDGotaFCeZ/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==), religion, food, discipline and medical care. Now multiply that by twenty adults with twenty different childhoods.
P28: Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once there are children in the middle of the disagreement. Communities need enough shared principles about raising children to offer coherence, and enough room for parents to still be parents.
